The proposed project is focused on responding to the challenges faced by pastoral and agro-pastoral women and men in Kotido District of Karamoja sub-region of Uganda, who live in chronic poverty, food, and income insecurity perpetuated by climate change and its injustices. Pastoral women and men are faced with Limited production and consumption of climate-resilient nutrient-dense foods, coupled with limited engagement in food system policy implementation. This has been exacerbated by the limited access to markets and value chain development services for crop and animal products, limited access to financial services, Knowledge gap, Weak capacity of local institutions and the private sector, and poor market systems.
In the Kotido District of Karamoja, where the proposed project will be implemented, Poverty is still a major obstacle to socio-economic development, most especially in the semi-arid Karamoja sub-region located in north-eastern Uganda, standing at 66% (having increased from 61% in 2017) with an estimated population of 1.8 millionpeople . Additionally, only 30% of persons aged 10 years or above are literate, while 66% of the persons aged 15 years or above have no formal schooling background. A commensurate rise in armed criminality, in which acts of violence are increasingly orchestrated irrespective of community norms on the use of force, has severely impaired the region’s socio-economic development. The root to these lie in a combination of political, socioeconomic, and ecological factors that include a long history of socioeconomic and political inequalities and marginalization by central authorities; Cross border proliferation of Small Arms and Light Weapons; Conflict legacies, and disarmament inadequacies; Commercialization of cattle rustling; unemployment; Changing land use, management, and development policies/ intervention in the region; Mineral exploration, oil discovery, and extractives.
Food insecurity has become a major and ongoing challenge with heavy reliance on the natural resources base, rendering livelihoods sensitive to climate dynamics. The overall food security situation in the region has deteriorated, with high food insecurity, increasing from 27% in June 2020 to 30% in April 2021, 41% in April 2022, 45% in May 2023, and 45% in 2024 in the Karamoja region with Moroto and Napak districts in Karamoja classified in the integrated food security phase classification (IPC) Phase 3 (Crisis), with Moroto 30% of the population (38,640 people), and Napak 40% (67,480 people) faced with high levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) in the region. The deterioration of food insecurity is attributed to multiple shocks, including dry spells from three consecutive poor seasonal rainfall performances (all below the five-year average), below-average crop and livestock production, localized resource-based conflict (cattle rustling), and the ripple effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, which resulted in increasing staple food prices across the east African region. The effects of unreliable rainfall patterns have led to poor harvests, post-harvest losses, and low seed quality, high incidences of crop/livestock pests and diseases, which in turn lead to low crop/livestock productivity and production. Ultimately, this has led to limited food availability, culminating in food insecurity. Karamoja is part of the expansive rangelands referred to as the “cattle corridor” which traverses East Africa from north to south, dominated by natural grassland, bushland, and woodlandsand is renowned for pastoralism, several ecological, administrative, social, economic, political and technological factors still constrain rangeland management and impact negatively on the welfare of the local people of Karamoja. Traditionally, rangelands were best utilized by nomadic pastoralists, and these livestock-based livelihoods are still considered the best economic foundation for households in the rangeland areas (draft Uganda RMPP 2013) . These harsh catchment conditions have forced pastoralists to be mobile; a practice that has relegated pastoralism to “second-class” status to crop farming, with a limited future and heading toward an inevitable transition to ranching, farming, or other alternative livelihoods. In the drought-prone Karamoja, pastoralists annually herd their cattle to water points and pastures, based on annual weather cycles and prevailing climatic conditions. The WSF2018 study confirms the fact that pastoralists are changing and adapting in several ways. Therefore, climate-resilient agriculture stands as the mostimportant coping strategy of the pastoralists under threat and should be openly promoted in order to insulate them from the advancing effects of climate change. WSF proposed project Is focused on Using local structures such as; Agro-Pastoral Farmer Field School (APFS) / approach, Opinion leaders, Council of elders; Traders’ associations; and Community Animal Health Workers (CAHWs) and networks as a platform for integration is not only an approach but also a strategy for sustainability that will ensure the continuation of benefits from the interventions after they are completed. It provides a Centre where multiple key stakeholders converge naturally and where ownership of project interventions can be more directly addressed. WSF will ensure community engagement in all aspects of the project to ensure ownership and sustainability of project outcomes. It provides a Centre where multiple key stakeholders converge naturally and where ownership of project interventions can be more directly addressed. WSF will ensure community engagement in all aspects of the project to ensure ownership and sustainability of project outcomes.
The Agro-pastoral Field Schools (APFS) approach adopted by the project is not only a strategy but a sustainability measure. The approach is a group-basedadult learning approach that teaches farmers how to experiment and solve problems independently. Sometimes called “schools without walls”, in APFS, groups of farmers meet regularly with a facilitator, observe, talk, ask questions, and learn together. Each APFS group will consist of 20-25 farmers and will be meeting once a week in a local field setting and under the guidance of a trained facilitator/Community Extension Worker (CEW) identified from the community. Community extension workers (CEWs)/AFFS facilitators will play a very significant role in reinforcing the extension systems, introducing new ideas through guided exercises, and stimulating discussion “by farmers, for farmers” without dominating the scene. The CEWs will support the identification of participants, develop AFFS curriculum and training plans, facilitate interactive and participatory learning sessions, provide technical guidance on agricultural practices, encourage experiential learning through hands-on activities, Foster critical thinking and problem-solving skills, promote group discussions and peer-to-peer learning. Monitor and evaluate AFFS impacts; Provide follow-up support and mentorship to communities and key structures on key activities; Facilitate linkages with input suppliers, buyers, and other stakeholders; Document and share best practices and build partnerships with local organizations and stakeholders. To enhance their effective engagement in the implementation of the project activities, the AFFS Facilitators will be provided a monthly stipend based on performance.
To make training easier and more practical, WSF has adopted and will utilize the “Smart Projector approach” in training farmers in targetedintervention areas. The “Smart projector” is a technology that has been developed by Access Agriculture, which is a non-profit organization, to enhance farmers' knowledge and skills through interactive video-based training. They use community extension agents known as Community Extension Workers (CEWs), who are either individuals or small teams that use a ‘smart projector’ to develop or expand their businesses around the dissemination of agricultural videos on farming and food processing across the global South. WSF believes that by building on the ICT skills and networks of young men and women, we can better support farmers, make organic agriculture more attractive to youth, and reach more women. The “Smart Projector” is a device pre-loaded with agricultural videos in various local languages, including Nga-karimojong . These models have already been proven and tested in communities and have had a tremendous impact. Furthermore, the smart Projector is solar-powered and can be used off-grid to train farmers using videos. The projector includes a Smart Projector, Remote, and Keyboard - use it as a computer, you can type and create documents. Bluetooth Speaker for large gatherings; a Power Bank - with 1.5m cable for the projector; a Solar Charger - so you can charge the power bank, phones, and other PCs directly; a Tripod - place your projector anywhere; and a Lockbox - protective, dust, and waterproof.
The cash for work (C4W) approach, also adopted by the project is focused on addressing the basic needs, preventing negative coping mechanisms, while building or rehabilitating productive assets, reducing the impact of natural hazards, and promoting climate change adaptation and mitigation,enhancing livelihood resilience to shocks and crises, and thus helping to address food security in the medium and long term. Sincemoney will be transferred directly to the affected households, poor and vulnerable households will be able to spend money accordingto their needs and priorities. The willproject, therefore, stimulate the recovery of the local economy by creating short-term work,reintroducing income flow, and supporting local businesses through the purchase of construction materials and other goods. The targeted households will be able to register increased household income and be able to purchase food and non-food items locally.
To enhance community, buy-in, and ownership of the project, community mobilisation and sensitisation meetings will be conducted to discussthe purpose of theproject, reasons for selecting the community, beneficiary selection processes, the time that the project will take, its intended impact, and measurable outputs that are expected. The importance of letting the community understand the fact that the project will only reach specific members of the community and not the whole community directly will enable them to understand thefact that though they may not directly benefit as workers for the C4W project, they will benefit from the infrastructure. The project team will support the selection process of the C4W committee, which will be elected directly by the community, and the beneficiary list generated. After the registration of beneficiaries, work supervisors with basic education and skills in line with their rolesand responsibilities will be selected. Each supervisor is assigned to a group of beneficiaries and to a specific site (of C4W activities). Before they start the work, supervisors will be asked to sign a contract of service with WSF as the implementing agency. To enhance the performance of community road works supervisors, the project team will facilitate onsite training on basic communication, Leadership and responsibilities, Record keeping, Group formation and group dynamics, Safety and security, and Project management.
The project will therefore link project beneficiaries to mobile money service providers to enable them to acquire and register for mobile money (e.g., MTN or Airtel) so that money can be paid directly to their mobile phones.The project will utilise our online system, which is easy, quick, and cost-effective in making payments. In situations where the mobile money networks are not present /available, funds will be delivered to the beneficiaries directly in cash, calculated according to the number of days worked.

HISTORY Warrior Squad Foundation (WSF) is a foundation of teams of life savours formed in early 2005 by group of young men and women at a time when Karamoja was ravaged by cyclic conflicts as an Indigenous non-profit making Non-Governmental Organization registered in Uganda (INDR93422994NB) in 2011 to advance the rights of young people (children, youth, women and men) who suffer from poverty and its injustices through working with them to find lifelong solutions to the key challenges they face. WSF envisions a peacefuland just world free from poverty. Our mission seeks to empower the very poor, marginalized, and vulnerable people to overcome poverty and its injustices. 2. ACHIEVEMENTS With funding support from several donors, and international organizations that include: USAID,UNDP, the Open Society Initiative for Eastern Africa (OSIEA), GIZ, IIRR, OXFAM, IGAD, theInfectious Disease Institute (IDI) of Makerere University, the Independent Development Fund (IDF), Mennonite Central Committee (MCC), International Institute for Rural Reconstruction (IIRR),USAID/SAFE, Community Integrated Development Initiative (CIDI), and Save the Children (SCI), etc. WSF has implemented successful projects in the Karamoja sub-region of Uganda with an overall goal of contributing to the socio-economic development ofpastoral and agro-pastoral communities of Karamoja that have been successful including USAID-Ugandans for Peace Activity; Building Resilience in Conflict-affected and Fragile Communities of Karamoja (BRICK); promoting socio-economic development and peace in African borderlands; Promoting Sustainable Natural resource Use and management (SUNRUM), Fostering Sustainable and Resilient Livelihoods (SURL), rights to food, (pasture growing model); Fostering sustainable and resilience (F-SURE); peacebuilding and human rights; conflict/violence prevention and mitigation; Breaking barriers to livestock mobility for food security in Arid and semi-Arid Lands (ASALs) of Karamoja; Building viable and resilient livelihoods for pastoralists and agro-pastoralists of Karamoja; child rights Governance; Strengthening Social Accountability in Karamoja; promoting peace and reconciliation; USAID Program for accelerated control of Tuberculosis in Karamoja; USAID Local PartnerHealth Strengthening on TB; etc. Our actions have contributed to the reduction in the marginalization and long-term, sustainable development of the people of the Karamoja subregion. Increased engagement of poor and vulnerable men and women in governance, and enjoy sustainable Peace and security; Increased productivity, income, and food security among the very poor and vulnerable women and men; Increased resilience and adaptation of poor and vulnerable women and men to climate change, disaster risks and engaged in the governance of natural resources; Increased access to quality education and lifelong learning among poor and vulnerable young people in Karamoja; and Increased access to quality health services, poor and vulnerable women enjoy improved nutrition and are healthy. In addition to the above, our actions have also promoted a policy environment that is supportive of the ability of the poor and vulnerable women and men to make real choices aimed at promoting sustainable and resilient Livelihoods through awareness creation. WSF employs a bottom-up approach of working from the community, district, and national levels to foster an environment that respects and promotes the rights of pastoralists through enhanced participation, prevention, and response to violations. Both of these programs were designed to address the socio-economic, cultural, and democratic rights needs of the most marginalized and hard to reach that have achieved significant results in fostering the socio-economic development of poor and vulnerable women and men in Uganda. Our experience and history point to a strong WSF relationship and good knowledge of the subregion. It hasalso led us to firmly believe in taking a long-term approach, seeking to address causes as well assymptoms. We see policy frameworks inimical to rights intimately bound up with the choices available to individuals within the community, and we have built our programs/projects on an interlinked approach of long-term programming, advocacy, and humanitarian response where needed. This links well with our organizational approach, the ‘one-program approach’ which explicitly focuses on achieving change (‘results’) and views long-term development programmes, humanitarian response, advocacy, and campaigning as integral parts of the ‘toolkit’ available to us toachieve positive change. 3. INSTITUTIONAL PURPOSE WSF envisions a peaceful and just world free from poverty. Our mission seeks to empower the very poor, marginalized, and vulnerable people to overcome poverty and its injustices. Institutional objectives: a) To promote the rights of children, youth, and communities who suffer from poverty and its injustices. b) To promote a peaceful, stable, and democratic environment, through strategic advice, quiet lobbying, dialogue, high-level briefs, and public debate by engaging key policy actors, decision makers, and those who influence them. c) To influence the policy environment through the documentation of knowledge, conducting evidence-based proactive research and analysis to provide a basis for viable policy reforms and practical alternatives that enable the attainment of broadbased economic development and improvement of quality of life in Uganda.
FIELDS OFACTIVITY
Program thematic areas: Our interventions have been grouped in five strands -Right to: 1) be safe and Healthy, 2) have sustainable livelihood, 3) have essential services, 4) be heard, and 5) have an identity. WSF’s intended impact will be achieved throughthe main program areas: Governance – Peacebuilding and human rights, Livelihoods and food security, Natural resources – Environment and climate change, inclusive quality lifelong learning, health, and nutrition.
1. Governance – Peace and Human Rights: Our Governance – peace <(>&<)> Human rights program is focused on increasing the engagement of poor and vulnerable men and women in governance and enjoying sustainable Peace and security. Through promoting Governance and accountability, peacebuilding and conflict mitigation, and promotion and protection of human rights.
2. Food Security and Livelihoods (FSL) program: Livelihoods <(>&<)> climate changeis one of our core program areas, as stated above. We believe that everyone has a right to a sustainable livelihood. Our Karamoja Food Security and Livelihoods (FSL) program is focused on” contributing to long-term, sustainable food and income security in the region through Enhancing food and income security and resilience among female and male pastoralists and agro-pastoralists in the Karamoja region by 2030 by; Our work is focused on 1) food production systems (crops and Livestock) strengthening;2) Improving Market systems; and 3) Food System Advocacy.
3. Natural Resource – Environment and Climate Change Adaptation: Our Natural Resources—Environment <(>&<)> Climate Change adaptation is aimed at “Increased adaptation and resilience of pastoralists and agro-pastoralists (especially 60% women and girls) to climate change and their engagement in natural resource use governance through building the capacity of pastoral communities to respond and manage disasters; promotion of climate-smart technologies; and natural resource governance.”
4. Inclusive lifelong learning (Education). Our program is focused on increasing access to quality education and lifelong learning among poor and vulnerable young people in Karamoja. This is through promoting Technical and Vocational Skilling (TVS); Basic education, and Early Child Care and Development (ECCD) in poor and marginalized communities.
5. Health <(>&<)> Nutrition program: Our health and Nutrition program is focused on increasing access to quality health services, where poor and vulnerable women enjoy improved nutrition and are healthy. Key areas of focus include: Maternal Health; Sexual Reproductive Health; Malaria control; TB control; and promoting child Nutrition.
